articles.title: No Beauty Scores: Why AfterVue Doesn't Rate Your Face
articles.notes: Existing article. Slug proposed, not verified: replace the URL before scheduling. Confirm not already scheduled in the Mac 90-day calendar. Caption written from the title and brand rules, not the live text; read the article once before approving.

first.headline: No scores. No judgment. Just a preview.
first.sub: Why AfterVue never rates a face
first.caption:
A consult tool has no business rating anyone's face.

Some simulator apps attach a number to the person looking at the screen. A score feels objective, but it only reflects what its training data rewarded, and it lands on a patient who walked in with a different question entirely.

AfterVue was built without one. The app shows an illustrative AI preview of a treatment direction on the patient's own photo, labels it as an illustration, and stops there. No rating, no flaw detection, no improvement percentage. The conversation about what is realistic stays where it belongs, with the injector in the room.

Takeaway: if a vendor demo shows a score, ask what it is for. The honest answer is usually engagement, not care.

Read why we made that call:
{url}

second.headline: The number we refuse to show.
second.sub: A consult tool should never grade a patient
second.caption:
Patients already judge themselves. Their software should not join in.

A beauty score looks like data. It is a model's opinion, trained on images nobody in your practice chose, delivered to someone who is nervous about their appearance. Reporting on AI appearance ratings has raised concern about what those numbers do to younger users, and a consult room is the last place to add one.

Our article explains the choice AfterVue made: an illustrative preview of a direction, labelled as an illustration, with nothing attached that ranks or grades. It also suggests plain wording for your treatment pages so visitors know the preview carries no rating before they upload a photo.

Takeaway: say "no scores" on the page in words a patient would use. It is a trust signal that costs nothing.

{url}

first.headline: Patients see their after. Before.
first.sub: Answer the question on your own site
first.caption:
Patients are already typing the question. The only variable is whose site answers it.

Searches like "how will I look after a wrinkle relaxer" happen before anyone calls a practice. Most of those searches land on a consumer app or a filter, where the result is dramatic, unlabelled, and attached to someone else's brand.

The article makes a simple case: put the answer on your own treatment page. A visitor uploads a photo, sees an illustrative AI preview of a possible direction on their own face, and then taps through to your booking page. The preview is labelled as an illustration, the photo is not stored by AfterVue, and the booking stays yours.

Takeaway: the question is being asked either way. Answering it on your site keeps the next step with you.

{url}

second.headline: Set expectations before the first visit.
second.sub: A labelled preview does part of the consult's work
second.caption:
The best place to set expectations is before the first visit, not during it.

When a prospective patient previews a treatment direction on their own face and reads that it is an illustration, not a promise, they arrive at the consult with a realistic starting point. The injector spends less time undoing a filter result from a consumer app and more time on what is possible for this face.

That is the quieter benefit in this article. The preview on your site is a marketing feature, but it is also an expectation-setting tool. It hands the visitor to your booking page with the right framing already in place.

Takeaway: a labelled preview on your treatment page does part of the consult's work early, and it does it in your words.

first.headline: Patient photos are protected health information.
first.sub: A plain-English checklist for your photo workflow
first.caption:
Patient photos are protected health information, whether or not insurance is involved.

Most of the risk in a medspa's photo workflow sits in habits: a quick shot on a personal phone, a text to the injector, an iPad with a camera roll full of faces. None of it feels like a breach while it is happening.

The article is a plain-English checklist for before and after photos: consent that is specific and revocable, practice-owned devices locked to one app, no email or messaging for images, a retention rule someone can recite, and a vendor question about where every photo goes after the consult. It is general information, not legal advice.

Takeaway: open the Photos app on your consult iPad. If a patient face is there, start with that line of the checklist.

{url}

second.headline: Ask every vendor where photos go.
second.sub: The question owners skip on the checklist
second.caption:
The question to ask any vendor that touches a patient photo is where it goes afterward.

Our photo checklist covers consent, devices, and messaging, but the vendor question is the one owners skip. A preview tool, a documentation platform, a booking widget, and a chat app can each hold an image, and each one is another system to secure and cover under an agreement.

AfterVue's answer is that the photo is processed for an illustrative AI preview and then discarded. Nothing is stored by AfterVue, and a BAA is available on request. The checklist in the article gives you the same question in a form you can put to every other vendor in the room.

Takeaway: the fewer places a patient photo can live, the shorter your audit. Not legal advice, but a good place to start.

{url}

first.headline: Fix the page before buying traffic.
first.sub: Where medspa websites lose the visitor
first.caption:
Before you buy more traffic, check what the traffic is doing when it arrives.

A medspa website that does not convert usually fails at a few predictable points: treatment pages that describe rather than answer, booking that sits two taps too deep, a gallery of other people's results, and nothing for the visitor who is curious but not ready to call.

The article works through those points in order, with the fix for each. The most overlooked one is the last. Most visitors leave because they cannot picture the result on their own face, and no ad budget solves that.

Takeaway: fix the page before you blame the traffic. An illustrative preview on the treatment page gives the undecided visitor a reason to act on the first visit.

{url}

second.headline: Traffic is a denominator. Consults count.
second.caption:
Traffic is a denominator. Consults are the number.

It is easy to report visits and hard to report what happened next. This article lists the places a medspa site loses the visitor between arrival and booking, and most of them are design decisions rather than marketing ones: slow pages on a mid-range phone, a services page with twenty accordions, a booking button that only appears on desktop.

The one we spend the most time on is the moment of hesitation. A visitor reads two treatment pages and closes the tab because the question "what would this look like on me" went unanswered.

Takeaway: audit your treatment pages on a phone over mobile data, and count the taps to booking. Then decide whether the problem was ever traffic.

{url}

first.headline: Do not send patients to a filter.
first.sub: What to check before recommending any app
first.caption:
Pointing a patient to a consumer simulator app hands your consult to a stranger.

Generic simulator apps are built to be shared, so they lean dramatic. Many add a beauty score. The photo is stored under terms nobody in your practice has read, and the result comes back unlabelled, so the patient treats a filter as a forecast.

The article sets out what a medspa should check before recommending any app: whether it runs on the patient's own face, whether every image is labelled as an illustration, whether it computes a score, where the photo goes, and whose booking page it ends on.

Takeaway: if you want patients previewing treatments, host the preview on your own site, under your brand, with your rules. Anything else is a referral you do not control.

{url}

second.headline: Filters chase downloads. Previews answer to you.
second.sub: Host the preview under your own brand
second.caption:
The difference between a filter and a preview is who has to stand behind it.

A consumer app answers to its download numbers. A preview on a practice's website answers to the injector who will see the patient next week. That changes the design: conservative rather than dramatic, labelled as an illustration, no score, and a handoff to the practice's own booking page.

This article is the checklist for telling the two apart, written for owners who get asked "is there an app for that" at the front desk. It also explains why AfterVue never stores the photo and never books the consult itself.

Takeaway: the right answer to "is there an app" is "yes, on our site." Then make sure your site can say it.

{url}

articles.title: AI Before/After Preview vs. Photo Documentation Tools: What's the Difference
articles.notes: Existing article. Slug proposed, not verified: replace the URL before scheduling. Confirm not already scheduled in the Mac 90-day calendar. Caption written from the title and brand rules; read the article once before approving.

first.headline: Preview or documentation. Decide first.
first.sub: Two products, one label, opposite jobs
first.caption:
Two products share the label "AI before and after," and they do opposite jobs.

A documentation tool records what happened: standardized clinical photos after treatment, stored under consent, compared across visits. A preview tool illustrates what might happen: a possible treatment direction on the patient's own photo, before anything is done.

Practices buy the wrong one when the pain is not named first. If the problem is inconsistent photos and consent paperwork, you need documentation. If the problem is patients who cannot picture the result, you need a preview. Many rooms end up with both, and they should not be the same system.

Takeaway: name the pain before the demo. The article gives you the one-sentence test for each category.

{url}

second.headline: Preview images do not belong in the chart.
second.sub: Keep the illustration and the record apart
second.caption:
Preview images do not belong in the chart.

That line surprises some owners. If a tool generates a picture, surely it should be filed. But an illustrative AI preview is a conversation aid, not a clinical record, and treating it as one creates two problems: an image that could be read as a promised outcome sitting in the patient's file, and one more copy of a face to secure.

This article separates the two categories cleanly. Documentation platforms keep real photos under consent and compare visits. A preview tool like AfterVue generates an illustration, labels it, and discards the photo. Different jobs, different storage rules, different vendors.

Takeaway: ask every tool in your consult room which category it is in, and keep the outputs apart.

{url}

articles.title: Is a Wrinkle-Relaxer Simulator Accurate? What It Can Show
articles.notes: New article, cluster C, status draft on branch claude/seo-cluster-c-accuracy. Patient-facing article shared to a practice audience. Do not schedule until reviewed, merged and live.

first.headline: Accurate about one thing. Silent on others.
first.sub: What a preview can and cannot know
first.caption:
A good preview is accurate about one thing and silent about several others.

Patients ask whether a simulator is accurate. The honest answer, written for them in our new article, is that a photoreal preview edits their own photo in a plausible direction, and that is the one thing it knows. It does not know dose, placement, muscle strength, healing time, or how etched lines will respond. A still image cannot show movement, and a wrinkle relaxer works on movement.

For a practice, the useful part is the list of questions a patient should bring to the consult after seeing a preview, and the guidance on reading a slider: look at the middle, not the extremes.

Takeaway: share this with patients before the visit. A preview that arrives with its own limits attached makes the consult easier.

{url}

second.headline: Only the treated area should move.
second.sub: How to read a before/after slider
second.caption:
A preview should move only the treated area. Anything else is flattery.

One of the practical tests in our patient article: if a before/after slider brightens the whole image or smooths skin everywhere, it is not illustrating a treatment, it is editing a portrait. Eyes, bone structure, and skin texture should stay put.

That standard is how AfterVue tunes its previews, and it is why every image carries a label calling it an illustration rather than a predicted result. The article is written for patients searching "is a wrinkle relaxer simulator accurate," but it reads as the explanation an injector would give if the consult had ten spare minutes.

Takeaway: link the article from your treatment page. Honest limits are a stronger trust signal than a dramatic result.

{url}

articles.title: What to Measure on a Medspa Website: Consults, Not Traffic
articles.notes: New article, cluster F, status draft on branch claude/seo-cluster-f-measure. Do not schedule until reviewed, merged and live.

first.headline: Four numbers. Fifteen minutes a week.
first.caption:
Four numbers. Fifteen minutes a week. No analytics team required.

Booking starts, completed requests, consults held, treatments scheduled. The ratios between neighbours tell you where to work: many visitors but few starts means the page is the problem; many starts but few completions means the booking flow has friction; many consults held but few treatments is a consult-room issue, not a website one.

The new measurement guide walks through setting the first two up in Plausible or GA4 without a developer, the UTM rules that stop Instagram and Google Business Profile clicks from vanishing into "direct," and the call-tracking caveat most owners learn the hard way.

Takeaway: pick a day, pull the four numbers, change one thing, and look at the same four numbers next week. Resist adding metrics.

{url}

second.headline: Never put a name in an event.
second.caption:
An analytics event should never carry a name, a phone number, a photo, or a note.

That rule is the privacy section of our measurement guide, and it matters more for a medspa than for most businesses. Website data can be health information in the regulator's eyes, call recordings capture health details, and a free-text form field can leak a diagnosis into a dashboard nobody audits.

The guide shows what a preview tool adds to the funnel on those terms: three events, preview started, preview generated, booking click, each carrying only a generic treatment area. AfterVue sanitizes properties before anything leaves the browser, stores no photos, and records the booking click as the key event because it does not book consults.

Takeaway: if you would not want a vendor to read it, do not put it in an event.

{url}

articles.title: Medspa Consult Room Technology That Helps the Conversation
articles.notes: New article, cluster G, status draft on branch claude/seo-cluster-g. Do not schedule until reviewed, merged and live.

first.headline: Design the room, then buy the tools.
first.sub: Consult-room technology that helps the conversation
first.caption:
Every screen in a consult room either supports the conversation or competes with it.

Most searches for consultation software start with a feature list. Our new guide starts with the room: arrival and consent, photo capture on an iPad locked to one app, an illustrative preview on the patient's own photo with a slider the injector moves while they talk, the expectations discussion, and a handoff to the practice's own booking system.

Then it sorts the tools into five jobs: EMR, digital consent, photo documentation, predictive preview, and scheduling. Most problems come from asking one tool to do a job it was not built for.

Takeaway: if the injector is looking at the iPad more than at the patient, the room is designed wrong. Fix the workflow before you buy anything.

{url}

second.headline: Lock the consult iPad to one app.
second.caption:
Lock the consult iPad to one app. Here is the setting.

Apple's Guided Access limits an iPad to a single app and can disable the hardware buttons. Turn it on under Settings, Accessibility, Guided Access, set a passcode, open the consult app, and triple-click the top button to start. That one step removes the camera roll full of faces that fails most photo audits.

It is one of the practical setups in our consult-room guide, alongside putting the consent step before the camera, giving staff a short script, and keeping patient photos off personal phones. AfterVue's iPad consult mode is built for Guided Access, generates an illustrative preview, and stores nothing.

Takeaway: a practice-owned, locked iPad is the cheapest compliance upgrade in the building.

{url}

first.headline: The words to say before the camera.

first.caption:
Patients ask one question before a camera points at their face: is this photo private?

A spoken script to read before the camera opens, a written consent paragraph separate from treatment consent, and a third form for marketing use that the patient can revoke later.

It also covers why those three documents cannot share a signature line, with notes on the Illinois, Texas, and Washington biometric laws that sit on top of HIPAA. It is general information, not legal advice, and your attorney should review anything you adopt.

second.headline: Three consents. Three signature lines.
second.caption:
One signature line for treatment, preview, and marketing turns a good consult into a complaint.

Treatment consent covers care. Preview consent covers an illustrative AI preview and nothing else. A marketing authorization, on its own form with an expiration and a revocation line, covers real before and after photos in a gallery or an ad. Our consent-script article explains why the HIPAA marketing rules push you toward three documents, and gives you a draft of the middle one.

AfterVue puts a provider consent step on screen before the camera, so the script happens before any photo is taken. The photo generates the preview and is then discarded.

first.headline: Built for owners, not for patients.
first.sub: Medspa website design that earns the consult
first.caption:
Most medspa websites are built to impress another medspa owner.

The visitor who matters is on her phone, between two other tabs, deciding whether a consult is worth her afternoon. She arrives with three questions: is this the right treatment, will it look natural on me, and what happens if I book. Every page element either answers one or gets in the way.

The new design guide covers treatment pages that answer those questions, gallery rules on consent and labelling, booking that is never more than one tap away, and Core Web Vitals and WCAG 2.1 AA as acceptance criteria rather than afterthoughts. Then it names the element most sites lack.

Takeaway: test the full booking flow on a mid-range Android phone over mobile data before you sign off on a redesign.

{url}

second.headline: Plan the preview into the redesign.
second.sub: A brief you can hand to any agency
second.caption:
If you are redesigning anyway, plan where the preview sits on each treatment page now.

Visitors leave because they cannot picture the result on their own face. A gallery shows someone else. A consult shows them, but only after they commit an afternoon. A preview widget closes that gap: the visitor uploads a photo, picks a treatment area, and sees an illustrative AI preview of a likely direction before deciding whether to book.

Our website design guide includes a brief you can hand to any designer or agency, with the preview widget and its privacy behaviour spelled out alongside the gallery rules and the ownership questions about your domain, hosting, and analytics.

Takeaway: a custom site is an asset. Make sure the domain, the code, and the content are yours before you sign.

{url}
